narration.full_text: Namaste, students! Today, we're diving deeper into solving systems of linear equations using the powerful elimination method. We'll also tackle some interesting word problems, transforming real-world scenarios into mathematical models that we can solve. Let's begin by mastering the elimination method. Our first example is solving the system: x + y = 5 and 2x - 3y = 4. To use elimination, we need the coefficients of one variable to be opposites. Here, if we multiply the first equation by 3, the 'y' terms will become 3y and -3y, which will cancel out when added. So, Equation 1 becomes 3(x + y) = 3(5), which simplifies to 3x + 3y = 15. Now we have two equations: 3x + 3y = 15 and 2x - 3y = 4. Let's add them together. (3x + 3y) + (2x - 3y) = 15 + 4. This simplifies to 5x = 19. From this, we can easily find x. x = 19/5. Now that we have the value of x, we can substitute it back into one of the original equations to find y. Let's use the first equation: x + y = 5. Substituting x = 19/5, we get (19/5) + y = 5. To solve for y, subtract 19/5 from both sides: y = 5 - 19/5. To perform this subtraction, find a common denominator, which is 5. So, y = (25/5) - (19/5). This gives us y = 6/5. Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is x = 19/5 and y = 6/5.
